title: 5,300-Year-Old Mummy's Secret Ingredient: Sourdough Bread!
summary:
Imagine opening a 5,300-year-old freezer and finding the world's oldest sourdough starter! That’s kind of what happened when scientists looked at Ötzi the Iceman. Ötzi is a prehistoric man found frozen in the Alps in 1991. His body had special yeasts that love the cold. These tiny microbes snuck into him after he died and stayed alive all this time. The scientists scooped some out and used them to bake bread. They said the sourdough was 'very very good.' Yum!

In other cool news, some Italian teenagers were working out in their school gym when they found something amazing underneath — an 1,800-year-old Roman house! Imagine doing jumping jacks and discovering ancient history below your feet.

And here’s a weird one: Google wants to release 64 million mosquitoes across the U.S. But don’t swat yet — these are boy mosquitoes that don’t bite. They carry a special bacteria that stops baby mosquitoes from growing. This could help stop diseases like West Nile virus. The government is deciding if it’s okay.

Oh, and scientists found the oldest rock art in the U.K. — it’s 17,000 years old! Plus, NASA said goodbye to its MAVEN spacecraft at Mars. It went quiet last December and is now officially lost. What a week of wild discoveries!
why_it_matters: These wild discoveries show that history is buried under our feet, tiny microbes can make delicious bread, and exploring space always teaches us something new.

background_read: Ötzi the Iceman is a 5,300-year-old mummy found frozen in the Alps, so well‑preserved that scientists could study his last meal.
Male mosquitoes don’t bite – only females need blood to lay eggs – so releasing millions of males is a clever way to fight diseases without harming people.
The MAVEN spacecraft (a NASA robot that orbited Mars studying its air) stopped communicating in December 2024 and is now officially considered lost.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ötzi the Iceman, Italian teenagers, scientists, Google, and NASA

WHAT: Discovering ancient yeasts used to bake sourdough, finding a Roman house under a school gym, planning to release 64 million harmless male mosquitoes, uncovering 17,000‑year‑old rock art, and losing the silent MAVEN spacecraft
WHERE: In the Alps, under an Italian school gym, across the U.S., in the U.K., and at Mars
WHY: To explore history, exercise, stop West Nile virus, study ancient art, and learn about the Red Planet

perspectives.description: Finding a 5,300‑year‑old sourdough starter or a Roman house under a school is thrilling because it connects us to people who lived thousands of years ago.
Releasing millions of mosquitoes might sound scary, but scientists say male ones don’t bite, and it could stop West Nile virus. Still, the government must check if it’s safe first.
These discoveries might make kids want to become archaeologists, biologists, or astronauts one day to uncover more of the world’s and universe’s secrets.
